notes.24:7: Latin "Propitius sit mihi Dominus" ("May the Lord be merciful to me") is the Vulgate's characteristic rendering of the Hebrew oath formula "Far be it from me from the Lord."
notes.24:11: The Vulgate explicitly reads first-person "et cogitavi ut occiderem te, sed pepercit tibi oculus meus" ("and I thought to kill you, but my eye spared you"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is often taken impersonally ("some said to kill you") and omits "my eye."
notes.25:2: The Vulgate reads "in solitudine Maon" ("in the desert of Maon"), specifying the desert where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has simply "in Maon."
notes.25:6: Latin "Sit fratribus meis et tibi pax" ("May peace be to my brothers and to you") preserves a distinctly Vulgate reading ("to my brothers") where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "to the living" or "for long life."
notes.25:22: Latin "mingentem ad parietem" ("one who urinates against a wall"; also in 25:34) literally renders an ancient idiom meaning any male.
notes.25:25: The Vulgate reads "dominus meus rex" ("my lord the king"), including the title "king" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has only "my lord."
notes.25:26: Latin "et salvavit manum tuam tibi" ("and saved your hand for you") is a distinctly Vulgate clause where the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of keeping David from avenging himself by his own hand.
notes.26:3: The Vulgate here transliterates Hebrew gib'ah ("hill") as the place name Gabaa ("Gibeah"), contrasting with in colle Hachila ("on the hill of Hachilah") in 26:1.
notes.26:5: The Vulgate adds clam ("secretly") and renders Hebrew bamma'gal ("encampment" or "barricade") as in tentorio ("in the tent," also in 26:7).
notes.26:10: Translating Hebrew ki im ("surely") literally as quia nisi ("unless"), the Vulgate links verse 10 grammatically to verse 11, where propitius sit mihi Dominus (literally "may the Lord be merciful to me") is the Vulgate idiom for "far be it from me."
notes.26:14: Distinct from the Hebrew ("who call to the king"), the Vulgate adds et inquietas ("and disturb"), using the same verb that Samuel speaks in 28:15.
notes.26:20: The Vulgate reads coram Domino ("before the Lord"), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "away from the presence of the Lord."
notes.27:7: A notable Vulgate reading: Latin quatuor mensium gives only "four months," whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "a year [lit. days] and four months."
notes.27:8: The Vulgate renders this clause as referring to rural districts or villages (pagi) inhabited from ancient times, whereas the Hebrew refers directly to the named peoples as ancient inhabitants of the land.
notes.27:12: The Vulgate translates literally as working many evils (Multa mala operatus est) against Israel, whereas the Hebrew uses an idiom meaning "he has made himself utterly odious" to his people.
notes.28:6: The Vulgate renders Hebrew ba'urim ("by Urim") as per sacerdotes ("through priests"), reflecting the priestly role in consulting the sacred lot.
notes.28:7: The Vulgate uses the Greek loanword python (an oracular or divining spirit, originally linked to the Pythian oracle) for Hebrew ov ("ghost" or "familiar spirit"), and similarly in pythone in 28:8.
notes.28:13: The Vulgate preserves the plural noun and participle (Deos ... ascendentes) of Hebrew elohim olim, referring to supernatural or spirit beings rising from the earth, even though Saul asks about a single figure in 28:14.
notes.28:16: The Vulgate reads that the Lord has passed over to Saul's rival (David), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "and has become your adversary." In 28:17, the Vulgate also uses future verbs and tibi ("to you") where the Hebrew uses past tense and "for himself."
notes.28:20: The Vulgate reads tota die illa ("all that day"), omitting "and all night" found in the Masoretic Hebrew. In 28:24, the Vulgate similarly renders the Hebrew "fattened calf" as vitulum pascualem ("pasture-fed calf").
notes.29:2: Latin satrapae ("satraps") reflects the distinct Philistine title (Hebrew seranim), whereas the Vulgate uses principes ("leaders") in verses 3, 4, and 9 for the Philistine commanders.
notes.29:5: Latin in millibus suis ... in decem millibus suis ("in his thousands ... in his ten thousands") preserves the Vulgate's literal rendering of the Hebrew idiom for Saul's thousands and David's ten thousands.
notes.29:6: The Vulgate joins et bonus in conspectu meo ("and good in my sight") to rectus es tu ("you are upright") and makes David's going out and coming in a separate clause, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text makes his going out and coming in the subject of "good in my eyes."
notes.30:4: Latin donec deficerent in eis lacrimae ("until tears failed in them") is a Vulgate-distinct rendering where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "until there was no more strength in them to weep."
notes.30:13: The Vulgate includes a third question, et quo pergis? ("And where are you going?"), absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, and uses nudiustertius ("the day before yesterday," by inclusive reckoning for "three days ago").
notes.30:20: The Vulgate reads singular minavit ante faciem suam ("drove them before his face"), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("they drove them ahead of the other livestock").
notes.30:27: The Vulgate reads Jether, a distinct form corresponding to "Jattir" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.30:30: The Vulgate reads Arama (corresponding to "Hormah" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text) and translates the first element of Hebrew "Bor-ashan" or "Chor-ashan" as in lacu Asan ("in the cistern of Ashan," literally "cistern/lake of Ashan").
notes.31:1: Matches Latin 'ceciderunt interfecti' smoothly in battle context without using banned 'slain' or unidiomatic 'fell killed'.
notes.31:2: The Vulgate reads Irrueruntque ... in Saul ("rushed upon Saul"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "pursued closely after" or "overtook."
notes.31:9: The Vulgate reads plural in populis ("among the peoples") and has no possessive pronoun with in templo idolorum ("in the temple of idols"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in the house of their idols and to the people."
notes.31:13: The Vulgate reads in nemore Jabes ("in the grove of Jabesh"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh."

unplaced.text: Saul was a son of one year when he began to reign, and he reigned over Israel for two years.
unplaced.note: The Vulgate renders a difficult Hebrew idiom literally as "a son of one year," often explained as a missing numeral or the start of Saul's kingship.

unplaced.text: Now David was the son of the Ephrathite man who was mentioned above, from Bethlehem of Judah, whose name was Jesse, who had eight sons; and in the days of Saul the man was old and advanced in years among men.
Now his three oldest sons went after Saul into battle; and the names of his three sons who marched out to war were Eliab the firstborn, the second Abinadab, and the third Shammah.
David, however, was the youngest. So when the three oldest had followed Saul,
David went away and returned from Saul to pasture his father's flock in Bethlehem.
Meanwhile the Philistine came forward morning and evening, and took his stand for forty days.
Now Jesse said to his son David, "Take for your brothers an ephah of roasted grain and these ten loaves of bread, and run into the camp to your brothers,
and bring these ten rounds of cheese to the commander; visit your brothers to see if they are doing well, and learn with whom they are stationed."
Now Saul, and they, and all the sons of Israel were fighting against the Philistines in the Valley of the Terebinth.

So David rose early in the morning, entrusted the flock to a keeper, and set out carrying his load, just as Jesse had commanded him. And he came to the place Magala and to the army, which had gone out to battle and had shouted in the combat.
unplaced.note: The Vulgate treats the Hebrew word for "encampment" or "entrenchment" as a place name, Magala.

unplaced.text: For Israel had drawn up its battle line, and the Philistines too had been prepared on the opposite side.
So leaving the supplies he had brought under the charge of the keeper at the baggage, David ran to the place of combat and asked whether everything was going well with his brothers.

And while he was still speaking with them, that man of illegitimate birth appeared coming up—Goliath by name, a Philistine from Gath—from the camp of the Philistines; and as he spoke these same words, David heard them.
unplaced.note: Latin spurius ("illegitimate") reflects Jerome's rendering of the Hebrew term for a single-combat champion ("man of the in-between").

unplaced.text: Now all the Israelites, when they saw the man, fled from before him, fearing him greatly.

And someone from Israel said, "Have you seen this man who has come up? For he has come up to taunt Israel. Therefore the king will enrich with great riches the man who strikes him down, and will give him his daughter, and will make his father's house exempt from tribute in Israel."

And David spoke to the men who were standing with him, saying, "What will be given to the man who strikes down this Philistine and takes away the disgrace from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, who has taunted the battle lines of the living God?"
And the people repeated the same report to him, saying, "These things will be given to the man who strikes him down."

When his oldest brother Eliab heard this while he was speaking with others, he grew angry with David and said, "Why have you come, and why have you left those few little sheep behind in the wilderness? I know your pride and the wickedness of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle."
And David said, "What have I done? Is it not a word?"
unplaced.note: Latin verbum ("word") reflects Hebrew davar, which can mean either a spoken word (a mere question) or a matter and reason.

unplaced.text: And he turned slightly away from him toward another and spoke the same words; and the people gave him an answer just as before.
Now the words that David spoke were heard, and were reported in the presence of Saul.
Now the Philistine walked on, advancing and drawing near against David, with his armor-bearer before him.
And David prevailed against the Philistine with a sling and a stone, and struck the Philistine and killed him. And since David had no sword in his hand,

Now at the time when Saul had seen David going out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, "From what lineage does this young man descend, Abner?" And Abner said, "As your soul lives, king, I do not know."
unplaced.note: Latin literally reads "Your soul lives, king, if I know," a Hebrew oath idiom expressing an emphatic denial.

unplaced.text: And the king said, "You inquire whose son this youth is."
And when David had returned after striking down the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him into Saul's presence, while David held the Philistine's head in his hand.
And Saul said to him, "From what family are you, young man?" And David said, "I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite."
And it happened that when he had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was closely bound to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
And Saul took him on that day and did not permit him to return to his father's house.
Now David and Jonathan entered into a covenant, for he loved him as his own soul.
For Jonathan stripped off the tunic he was wearing and gave it to David, along with the rest of his garments, even to his sword and his bow, and even to his belt.

David also went out to everything for which Saul sent him, and conducted himself prudently; and Saul placed him over the men of war, and he was pleasing in the eyes of all the people, and especially in the sight of Saul's servants.

Now the day after, an evil spirit of God seized Saul, and he was prophesying in the middle of his house, while David was playing music with his hand, just as he did each day. And Saul was holding a spear,
unplaced.note: The Vulgate uses "prophetabat" ("was prophesying") here rather than a verb meaning "raved."

unplaced.text: and he threw it, thinking that he could pin David to the wall; and David turned aside from his presence a second time.

And Saul said to David, "Here is my older daughter Merab. I will give her to you as a wife; only be a brave man and fight the battles of the Lord." But Saul was reasoning, saying, "Let my hand not be against him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him."
But David said to Saul, "Who am I, or what is my life, or the clan of my father in Israel, that I should become the king's son-in-law?"
But when the time came that Merab, the daughter of Saul, should have been given to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite as a wife.
And the princes of the Philistines went out. Now from the beginning of their going out, David conducted himself more prudently than all the servants of Saul, and his name became greatly renowned.
unplaced.note: Literally rendering the Vulgate's "A principio autem egressionis eorum" ("from the beginning of their going out").

unplaced.text: And David said, "Will the men of Keilah deliver me and the men who are with me into the hands of Saul?" And the Lord said, "They will deliver you over."
